newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Effective new Russian tax code seems unlikely soon.
newsitem.headline: Effective new Russian tax code seems unlikely soon.

text.p: A new Russian tax code, promised by the government as a key to improving economic efficiency and attracting investment, appears unlikely to be passed this year.
But some business analysts said on Friday that, despite pressure from the IMF for a new code, investors should not attach undue significance to slow progress on its introduction.
Russian industry is suffocating under a complex and unfair tax system cobbled together during post-Soviet Russia's five-year slog towards a market economy.

"You need a tax code in this country," Michel Camdessus, managing director of the International Monetary Fund, bluntly told members of parliament this week. "If not, forget about having the huge resources you need for this country."

High but unequal taxes and patchy enforcement have created a messy situation where a few taxpayers pay extremely high rates and others pay none at all, leaving the government gasping for funds with revenue receipts well below target.
Regional taxes are unequal and can also be high, while harsh penalties face those who disagree with tax inspectors' often unpredictable interpretations of vague rules, accountants say.

Camdessus asked the opposition-led State Duma lower house to pass the tax code and said the IMF, which has delayed some tranches of a three-year $10-billion loan over tax shortfalls, would send no funds until the government submitted the bill.
But the administration, which is still working on the code, and the communist-dominated Duma, which has refused to consider it piecemeal, have serious disagreements.
President Boris Yeltsin and First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, recently appointed to spearhead new economic reforms, have both said a tax code is a high priority.
But Yeltsin, who has ordered the draft be submitted by the end of April, left tax legislation off an official list of legislative priorities that he passed to the Duma on Friday.
"It probably will not be completely in effect before 1999," said Gennady Kulik, deputy chairman of the Duma budget and tax committee and a member of the communist-allied Agrarian party.
Top reformers agree the code will not pass.

Duma member Oxana Dmitriyeva, head of the budget sub-committee and a member of the Yabloko liberal opposition party, said the draft code treated taxpayers unequally and failed to regulate the tax service -- two IMF criticisms.
She said dissatisfied reformers did not want to pass the code without improvement and some Duma members were reluctant to vote for a code cutting privileges to pet industries.
"It would be bad if the Duma passes the tax code," she said.
But Vladimir Gurevich, deputy economic editor at the weekly Moscow News, said the tax code's importance was overstated.
The draft code is not radical, he said, tax evaders would find ways around whatever new rules were drawn up in any case.

"It is a symbol, more than an instrument." But he said lack of a tax code would force the Duma to pass an unrealistic 1998 budget analagous to the 1997 version which took months to pass and was adopted after the calendar year had begun.
Kevin Norville, a tax specialist at Deloitte & Touche in Moscow, said the code would be helpful but that investors and tax payers would struggle along under the old system if need be.
"I have not heard anybody give it as a reason not to come in to (invest in) Russia," he said.
